abstract: Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.
